doc.title: Programming in C
doc.paragraph: Most of what you write in C for Adaptive Framework, whether it is a function, an adapter or a whole command, comes down to the same few things: making values, keeping the ones you need, letting go of the ones you don't, and turning text into strings and back. This chapter goes over the rules for each. The Doxygen pages for C developers, and the Runtime model page in particular, have the same rules in reference form, and the headers have the details for each function.

section.title: Where a Value Lives
section.paragraph: Every value is a const afw_value_t *, but not every value lives the same way. Most of the memory your code uses is temporary. It comes from the pool you were given, usually called p, and it goes away all at once when that pool goes away. Let's look at a function that returns a digest, a simplified version of one from the afw_crypto extension:

Everything here is made in x->p, the pool the caller passed in. The function never frees any of it and the caller never releases the result: it lasts as long as x->p does. We call this pool the dest p. Always pass the dest p you were given. Do not use xctx->p as a place to put things just because it is handy, since it can last much longer than the work you are doing.
Values, objects and arrays come in four kinds, and the name of the function that creates one tells you which kind you get:

row.column: Permanent
Compiled in, such as afw_value_null, or registered constants
As long as the environment
Pooled
Until the pool it was made in goes
Reference counted
create_unmanaged_new_p, create_unmanaged_cede_p
In a pool of its own, until its last reference is released
Fully managed
In p->managed_p, until its last reference is released

section.paragraph: Values, objects, arrays and pools all share the afw_reference interface: get_reference(instance, xctx) takes a reference, and release(instance, xctx) lets go of one. For a permanent value both do nothing. A pooled value has no references at all, so both throw. If you need a pooled value to outlive its pool, ask for a copy you can keep (see below).

section.title: Who Releases
section.paragraph: The rule at the edge of every function is simple: a function does not release its parameters, and its caller does not release its result. That covers afw_value_evaluate(), the execute function of every Adaptive function, every afw_compile_* function, and the getters that return a property or an entry from an object or array. What they return lasts for the dest p. If a function returns a fully managed value, it is the function's job to register that value's release on the caller's pool.
A few calls hand you a reference, and then you release it when you are done:

list.item: Every create_managed function, such as afw_object_create_managed() and afw_array_create_managed().
afw_value_get_reference() (and the object and array forms), when you want to keep this exact instance. Release it through the same interface you got it from.

afw_value_get_assignable_value(value, p, xctx), when you want a value you own and can store. A pooled value comes back as a fully managed copy, and a counted value comes back as itself with one more reference.

section.paragraph: If you only need a value to last as long as some pool, use afw_value_get_for_p_lifetime(value, p, xctx) instead. It registers the release on p for you, so there is nothing to release.

When you put a value you own into an object or array, afw_object_set_property_take() and afw_array_push_value_take() take your reference along with the value, so you do not release it afterwards. The plain afw_object_set_property() and afw_array_push_value() add a reference of the container's own, and you still release yours.

One more case is worth knowing about. If you read a property or an entry and then call something that runs user code, such as a script function passed in as a callback, that code can replace the property and free the value you are holding. Hold it first with afw_value_hold_read(value, p, xctx), which keeps it alive until p goes.

To copy a value, choose the function by what you want the copy for. afw_value_clone() makes an independent copy that a script may change, the same as Adaptive Script's clone(); you release it. afw_value_to_managed() gives you a fully managed version, sharing the original when it already is one; you release it. afw_value_create_pooled_copy() makes a plain copy in p, for taking a value out of data that might change; you do not release it. Each has afw_object_ and afw_array_ forms.

section.title: Pools
section.paragraph: You will seldom need a pool of your own, but when you do, afw_pool_create(parent, xctx) makes one like its parent. Allocate from any pool with afw_pool_malloc(), afw_pool_calloc() and afw_pool_free_memory(), always passing the pool. Freeing the same block twice throws. Release a pool you made with afw_pool_release(). Functions you register with afw_pool_register_cleanup() run when the pool goes, and must not throw.

section.title: Strings
section.paragraph: Text in Adaptive Framework is an afw_utf8_t: a pointer to the bytes and a length, with no terminating zero. The bytes are always valid UTF-8 in Unicode Normalization Form C (NFC), and never hold U+FEFF (the byte order mark). That is what lets two strings be compared byte by byte. The functions that make one check for that and throw if the text is not valid UTF-8. Their names tell you whether the bytes are copied:

row.column: A copy of the bytes in p, normalized to NFC.
A new afw_utf8_t that points at your bytes, which must outlive it. Throws if they are not NFC.
A copy of a zero-terminated C string.
Points at a zero-terminated C string without copying it.
afw_utf8_from_memory, afw_utf8_as_memory
Moves between text and an afw_memory_t of bytes.

section.paragraph: To set the fields of an afw_utf8_t you already have, use afw_utf8_set() (which copies) or afw_utf8_set_no_copy() rather than filling in .s and .len yourself.

section.title: Formatting Text
section.paragraph: afw_utf8_printf() and AFW_THROW_ERROR_FZ() use Adaptive Framework's own formatter, which adds a few format specifiers to the usual ones. The one you will use most is %ku, which takes a const afw_utf8_t *. Here is an example from the afw_lmdb extension:
section.code: AFW_THROW_ERROR_FZ(general, xctx, "Adapter '%ku' is not an LMDB adapter", adapter_id);

row.column: NULL prints nothing.
C string
For text that might not be valid UTF-8, such as an operating system or LDAP message. Bytes that are not valid are written as ^, hex and ^ instead of throwing.
The bytes, encoded the same way as %ks.
%kx, %kX
The bytes as lowercase or uppercase hex.
C string
Throws if the text is not valid UTF-8. In error messages it is encoded like %ks instead, so building an error never throws.

section.paragraph: AFW_UTF8_FMT and AFW_UTF8_FMT_ARG() are only for the C library's own functions, such as fprintf(). Do not use them with afw_utf8_printf() or AFW_THROW_ERROR_FZ(): they pass two arguments where %ku expects one, which reads the wrong arguments and can crash. ./afwdev build --scan checks the formats.
These functions are for text people read, such as messages and logs. To write data, such as a file, put the text together yourself and write its bytes.
